title: From RAN insight to action: how rApps drive autonomous network operations
summary: How rApps work as AI agents to move RAN operations from insight to autonomous action.

Hashtags


[#rApps](https://www.ericsson.com/en/search?q=rApps)[#AutonomousNetworks](https://www.ericsson.com/en/search?q=AutonomousNetworks)[#EIAP](https://www.ericsson.com/en/search?q=EIAP)


A network automation platform is only worth what the network can do differently because of it. Today's mobile networks are carrying more traffic, more complexity, and more performance pressure than earlier generations were designed for. More bands, more sites, more layers. Purpose-built RAN, Cloud RAN, and Open RAN environments now sit side by side. Services carry more differentiated performance requirements and the volume of network data has passed the point where people can review it by hand and still act in time.


Adding another standalone tool does not fix this. It adds to the pile. What RAN teams actually need is a way to apply automation and AI consistently across the network lifecycle from one environment, with the intelligence to act, not just report.


That is the job of rApps: applications that run on a common automation platform and translate network insight into specific results. More than that, they are the building blocks of Autonomous RAN domain — a direct step on the path from today's manual operations toward the intent-driven, self-managing networks that define the next decade of telecoms.


Autonomous networks are not a single product or a switch you flip. They represent an operating model — one where closed loops, intent-driven control, and automated decision-making gradually take on the work that today requires manual effort and human judgment.


The TM Forum defines autonomy on a scale from Level 0 (fully manual) to Level 5 (fully autonomous). Most networks today operate between Level 2 and Level 3. Reaching Level 4 — where the network can interpret business intents and execute operational tasks with minimal human intervention — requires intelligent automation applied systematically across the RAN lifecycle.


rApps are how that happens in the RAN. They are the execution layer of autonomous networks at the radio access layer, running on the Ericsson Intelligent Automation Platform (EIAP) and turning data into open or closed-loop action across planning, deployment, optimization, and self-healing operations.


### How the platform and rApps fit together


The relationship is simple:


- The platform is the operating environment. EIAP includes a non-real-time RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) and a Developer Portal, and supports purpose-built RAN, Cloud RAN, and Open RAN. It is described accurately as the key enabler of autonomous networks at the RAN layer.
- rApps are the AI-powered applications that run on it.
- Network data is the input. Intent-driven, coordinated network action is the outcome.


Because these applications share one environment, the AI intelligence you build for one use case — the data pipelines, the trained models, the observability hooks — can be reused for the next, instead of rebuilt each time. That reuse is what makes automation compound: every use case adds to the platform's collective intelligence rather than sitting in a silo.


### What rApps do across the RAN lifecycle


This is where the value gets concrete. Think in four stages and a foundation that makes all four possible.


#### Plan and evolve


rApps support data-driven planning, dimensioning, and investment decisions. AI-powered analysis of network performance, traffic patterns, and coverage gaps means you put investment where it creates the most value and align network evolution with actual business priorities — not assumptions.


#### Deploy


rApps simplify complex rollouts and cut repetitive configuration work. That means faster site introduction, more consistent settings across the estate, and fewer manual handovers and errors. Automation that previously took weeks of engineering effort gets compressed into a controlled, repeatable process.


#### Optimize


rApps continuously analyze network behavior using AI models and recommend or directly apply improvements: better spectrum usage, smarter load distribution, improved user experience. Over time, the optimization loop tightens — the AI learns from results and refines its recommendations.


#### Heal


rApps detect anomalies, isolate likely root causes, and support closed-loop correction autonomously, without waiting for a manual fault ticket. Issues resolve faster, service impact drops, and operations shift from reactive firefighting to preventive self-healing. This is the capability that most clearly marks progress toward higher autonomy levels.


### Enabler rApps: the foundation underneath


Enabling the four lifecycle stages is a category that often goes unmentioned: Enabler rApps. These are not use-case applications — they are the foundational capabilities that other rApps depend on. Data collection, AI and ML model management, common observability services, and policy frameworks. Building on Enabler rApps means operational rApps get consistent, high-quality inputs and share common AI infrastructure rather than duplicating it. Think of them as the platform's operational nervous system.


### Why the ecosystem matters more than any single app


It would be easy to read this as a software catalog. The more important point is the ecosystem.


A shared platform lets service provider-built, third-party, and vendor applications run in the same place, on open interfaces and an SDK. Ericsson's rApp ecosystem has grown past 100 applications from more than 100 members across leading CSPs, alongside independent software vendors and academic institutions.


That gives service providers the freedom to tackle their own priorities without building every capability from scratch, and it means the innovation of the wider industry becomes available on the same platform where you already run your own automation.


### rApps as AI agents: intent, coordination, and conflict management


A fair question at this point: won't more rApps mean more complexity?


That is exactly what the platform exists to answer. Its role is to provide the governance, security, and coordination that stop applications from becoming disconnected islands — and this is where Agentic AI changes the picture.


Each rApp operates as an AI agent with a clear purpose: a specific operational goal, defined data inputs, and a set of permitted actions. Agents do not run in isolation. They operate under shared policies and observe common network intents — the high-level business and performance objectives the service provider has defined as the desired state of the network.


When those intents overlap or create tension, the platform's conflict management capability resolves them. This is the role of Intent Manager rApps — a new class of application currently under active development. An Intent Manager rApp acts as a coordination layer: it receives the objectives of multiple operational agents, identifies conflicts (for example, one agent optimizing for throughput while another conserves energy in the same cells), and determines which action best serves the overarching intent. The result is that automation across the RAN works in concert rather than at cross-purposes.


This architecture is how Agentic AI applies in the RAN specifically. It is not that individual rApps become 'AI-powered' in isolation — it is that a group of rApps, each operating as a purposeful agent, can be orchestrated through intent to behave as a coherent autonomous system. That is the step that moves operations from rule-based task execution to genuinely intent-driven autonomy.


### A practical path to RAN autonomy with rApps


Autonomy in the RAN is not all-or-nothing. A realistic sequence looks like this:


1. Pick one operational challenge with a measurable impact — a KPI gap, a recurring fault type, or a manual process that consumes engineering time.
2. Secure access to the network data it needs. This is where Enabler rApps and good data management earn their cost.
3. Deploy the relevant rApps for that use case.
4. Start with insight and recommendations — human-in-the-loop before any autonomous action.
5. Define the guardrails first. Add controlled actuation once you trust the results.
6. Close the loop and measure the outcome against the baseline.
7. Expand to adjacent use cases, reusing the data pipelines and AI infrastructure you have already built.
8. As multiple rApps operate across overlapping areas of the network, introduce intent management. Express the network objectives you want to achieve — performance, energy efficiency, experience — and let an Intent Manager rApp coordinate the agents toward those shared goals without conflicts or contradictory actions.


The last step is the most consequential. Individual rApps deliver use-case value. Intent management transforms a collection of use cases into a coordinated autonomous system — one where the network is continuously aligning its behavior to business outcomes, not just executing pre-defined rules.


RAN autonomy gets built one trusted use case at a time. The advantage scales when each use case stops being an isolated project and becomes part of a platform that reuses intelligence, coordinates agents through intent, and progressively raises the autonomy level of the entire network.
